blocks.content: Deployment models answered where infrastructure lives. This topic answers a genuinely different question: once you have decided to use the cloud, how much of the technology stack do you actually manage yourself, and how much does the provider handle?
1. IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Infrastructure as a Service, Platform as a Service, and Software as a Service describe three distinct layers at which a cloud provider can meet you, each drawing the line between what you manage and what the provider manages in a different place.

This is a spectrum, not three isolated categories. Moving from IaaS toward SaaS means handing progressively more operational responsibility to the provider, in exchange for progressively less control over the underlying implementation details.

Nearly every AWS service covered across the remaining eighteen modules of this course fits somewhere on this spectrum, and correctly identifying where a given service sits is genuinely useful for predicting exactly what you will and will not need to manage yourself.

This topic covers all three layers with concrete AWS examples, giving this otherwise abstract spectrum real, practical grounding before the very next topic formalizes the responsibility split with AWS's own official model.

blocks.content: 2. A Stack of Responsibility, Divided Differently by Each Layer
blocks.text: 2. A Stack of Responsibility, Divided Differently by Each Layer

blocks.content: Picture the full technology stack needed to run an application: physical hardware at the bottom, then virtualization and operating system, then runtime and middleware, then the application code itself at the top.
Infrastructure as a Service hands you everything from the operating system upward to manage yourself, with the provider handling only the physical hardware and virtualization layer beneath that.
Platform as a Service hands you only the application code layer to manage, with the provider handling the operating system, runtime, and middleware layers beneath that on your behalf.

Software as a Service hands you nothing to manage at the infrastructure or application layer at all. You simply use a fully built, fully managed application, with the provider responsible for every layer beneath it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736047252-182980913.png
blocks.alt: A stack of responsibility divided between you and the provider

blocks.content: 3. A Real IaaS, PaaS, SaaS Example
blocks.text: 3. A Real IaaS, PaaS, SaaS Example

blocks.content: Consider three ways to run a web application on AWS, each sitting at a different layer of this spectrum, illustrating the practical difference between the three models concretely rather than abstractly.

An EC2 instance is Infrastructure as a Service: you choose the operating system, install and configure a runtime, deploy your application code, and remain responsible for patching and maintaining the operating system yourself.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk is Platform as a Service: you provide only your application code, and Elastic Beanstalk handles provisioning the underlying servers, operating system patching, and runtime configuration entirely on your behalf.

A Gmail account, while not an AWS service, is a clear, universally familiar example of Software as a Service: you simply use a fully built email application, with the provider responsible for absolutely every layer beneath the interface you interact with.

# IaaS: you manage the OS and runtime yourself
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 --instance-type t2.micro

# PaaS: you provide only application code
eb create my-app-environment

blocks.content: 4. Recap: Where Infrastructure Lives Versus Who Manages What
blocks.text: 4. Recap: Where Infrastructure Lives Versus Who Manages What

blocks.content: The Cloud Deployment Models topic earlier in this module established where infrastructure physically lives and who shares access to it, public, private, or hybrid, a question this topic has deliberately left entirely unaddressed until now.

IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS answer a genuinely separate question, within whichever deployment model has already been chosen: how much of the technology stack running on top of that infrastructure do you actually manage yourself.

These two questions combine independently. A private cloud deployment can offer IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS just as a public cloud deployment can, and understanding them as two separate dimensions, rather than one combined choice, prevents a common source of confusion.

The very next topic, Shared Responsibility Model, formalizes exactly how this service model choice shifts security and operational responsibility between you and AWS, building directly on the stack of responsibility introduced in this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736050442-734932186.png
blocks.alt: Recap of where infrastructure lives, now examined for who manages what

blocks.content: 5. Visualizing the Responsibility Stack

The four layer stack introduced earlier in this topic, application code, runtime and middleware, operating system and virtualization, and physical hardware, provides a genuinely useful visual for reasoning about any specific AWS service's actual position on this spectrum.

For any new AWS service encountered throughout the remaining eighteen modules of this course, asking which of these four layers you are actually responsible for managing is a fast, reliable way to correctly classify it as IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS like.

Many real world AWS services do not fit perfectly cleanly into just one of the three categories, and recognizing a service as sitting somewhere along this spectrum, rather than forcing it into exactly one label, is often the more accurate and more useful mental model.

This visual stack, established here early in the course, will be referenced again implicitly throughout later modules whenever a new managed service is introduced, making it worth genuinely internalizing now rather than treating as a one time definition.

blocks.content: 6. A Common Mistake: Defaulting to IaaS for Everything
blocks.text: 6. A Common Mistake: Defaulting to IaaS for Everything

blocks.content: A common mistake, especially among engineers with a strong traditional systems administration background, is defaulting to IaaS, such as raw EC2 instances, for every new application, without seriously considering whether a PaaS option would genuinely serve better.

This habit often stems from familiarity and a desire for maximum control, but it means taking on real, ongoing operating system patching and runtime management responsibility that a PaaS option like Elastic Beanstalk would otherwise handle automatically.

For many genuinely standard web applications, without an unusual, specific requirement demanding full operating system level control, a PaaS option delivers the same end result with meaningfully less ongoing operational burden.

The fix is a deliberate habit: for any new application, briefly evaluate whether a PaaS or even SaaS option genuinely fits before defaulting to IaaS out of familiarity, applying the same focus benefit already established in the Why Cloud topic earlier in this module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736053547-665623394.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of choosing IaaS for everything without considering PaaS simplicity

blocks.content: 7. Choosing the Right Layer for a Given Workload
blocks.text: 7. Choosing the Right Layer for a Given Workload

blocks.content: SaaS is the right choice when a fully built application already exists that meets your needs, and no meaningful customization or differentiation would come from building it yourself, exactly like the universally familiar Gmail example covered earlier in this topic.

PaaS is the right choice for most custom applications where your genuine value lies in the application code itself, not in managing the underlying operating system, runtime, or middleware, which is precisely why Elastic Beanstalk exists as a practical AWS option.

IaaS is the right choice specifically when a genuine requirement demands operating system level control, a highly customized runtime environment, or software that simply cannot run within a PaaS platform's more constrained, managed environment.

Applying this evaluation deliberately for every new workload, rather than defaulting reflexively to whichever layer is most familiar, is the practical skill this topic has been building toward across its examples and common mistake section alike.
8. Containers as a Layer Between IaaS and PaaS
blocks.text: 8. Containers as a Layer Between IaaS and PaaS

blocks.content: Containers, and container orchestration platforms such as AWS's own Elastic Kubernetes Service and Elastic Container Service, occupy a genuinely useful middle position on this spectrum, sitting between raw IaaS and fully managed PaaS.

With containers, you manage your application's runtime environment through a container image, but you no longer manage a full, persistent virtual machine operating system the way traditional IaaS requires, gaining meaningful operational simplicity without losing PaaS's typical runtime constraints.

This middle position has made containers extremely popular for teams wanting more portability and control than PaaS typically offers, while still avoiding the full operating system management burden that traditional IaaS carries.

Container based services are not covered in further depth in this introductory module, but recognizing where they sit on this spectrum now will make their fuller treatment, in Module 3, Compute Services, considerably easier to place correctly.
9. A Second Real Example: Content Management
blocks.text: 9. A Second Real Example: Content Management

blocks.content: Consider a company needing a corporate blog. A SaaS option, a fully hosted third party blogging platform, requires no infrastructure management at all but offers limited customization beyond what that platform natively supports.

A PaaS option, deploying a custom blog application through Elastic Beanstalk, offers considerably more customization and control over the actual application logic while still avoiding operating system and runtime management burden.

An IaaS option, running that same blog application on a raw EC2 instance with full manual configuration, offers maximum control, useful if the blog needs a highly customized server environment that a PaaS platform's more constrained environment cannot accommodate.

This example, alongside the earlier EC2, Elastic Beanstalk, and Gmail example, reinforces the same evaluation pattern from a genuinely different, more relatable everyday use case, making the spectrum concept easier to internalize through repetition across varied contexts.
10. Cost Implications Across the Spectrum

Generally, moving from IaaS toward SaaS trades a lower direct infrastructure cost, since you manage more yourself with less provider overhead, for a higher direct service cost, since the provider bears more of the operational burden on your behalf.

This is not a universal rule, since a PaaS or SaaS option can sometimes be genuinely cheaper overall once the real, often underestimated cost of your own team's operational time managing IaaS infrastructure is properly accounted for.

This connects directly to the total cost of ownership discussion in the Why Cloud topic earlier in this module: raw infrastructure price alone is rarely the complete picture, and staffing time spent on operational burden carries a genuine, real cost.

Evaluating cost across this spectrum honestly, accounting for both direct service cost and indirect operational time cost together, produces a more accurate picture than comparing raw infrastructure pricing alone.
11. Recognizing This Spectrum in Job Postings and Team Structures
blocks.text: 11. Recognizing This Spectrum in Job Postings and Team Structures

blocks.content: AWS engineering roles often implicitly specialize around different points on this spectrum: an infrastructure or platform engineering role frequently works closer to the IaaS end, while an application or product engineering role frequently works closer to the PaaS or SaaS end.

Recognizing this pattern is genuinely useful context for anyone building a career around AWS skills, since the specific balance of infrastructure versus application focus varies meaningfully between organizations and between specific roles within the same organization.

This course covers services across the entire spectrum, since a well rounded AWS engineer benefits from understanding all three layers even if their own day to day work concentrates primarily on just one of them.

This broader context is worth keeping in mind as later modules introduce increasingly specific services, helping frame where each new service sits both technically and in terms of the kind of role that typically works with it most directly.
12. This Spectrum Across the Rest of This Course
blocks.text: 12. This Spectrum Across the Rest of This Course

blocks.content: Module 3, Compute Services, covers EC2 and other IaaS offerings in full depth. Module 12, Serverless Architecture, covers AWS Lambda, arguably sitting even further along this spectrum than traditional PaaS, since you manage neither servers nor a persistent runtime environment.

Many of AWS's managed database services, covered in Module 5, sit closer to the PaaS end of the spectrum as well, handling operating system patching, backups, and replication automatically while still giving you meaningful configuration control over the database itself.

Recognizing this spectrum as a recurring, useful lens, rather than a concept specific to this one topic, will make evaluating new AWS services throughout the rest of this course meaningfully faster and more intuitive.

Every remaining module in this course implicitly assumes this topic's stack of responsibility framework as shared, established vocabulary for describing exactly what any given service actually requires you to manage.

13. Best Practices for Evaluating Service Model Choice
blocks.text: 13. Best Practices for Evaluating Service Model Choice

blocks.content: Ask, for every new workload, which layer of the responsibility stack genuinely needs to be under your own direct control, rather than defaulting to whichever layer is most familiar from prior experience.

Prefer PaaS or higher over IaaS whenever a workload's genuine value lies in application logic rather than infrastructure configuration, applying the focus benefit from the Why Cloud topic concretely to this specific decision.
Reserve IaaS for workloads with a genuine, specific requirement for operating system level control or a highly customized runtime that a PaaS platform cannot accommodate.

Revisit service model choices as a workload matures, since an application that started on IaaS for early flexibility may be a strong candidate for migration to PaaS once its runtime requirements have stabilized.

blocks.content: 14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS describe a spectrum of how much of the technology stack you manage yourself versus your provider manages on your behalf, a genuinely distinct question from where infrastructure physically lives, covered in the previous two topics.

Defaulting to IaaS out of familiarity, rather than deliberately evaluating whether PaaS or SaaS would better serve a given workload, is a common mistake that trades away real operational simplicity for control that is often not genuinely needed.

The next topic, Shared Responsibility Model, formalizes exactly how this service model choice shifts security responsibility between you and AWS, building directly on the stack of responsibility framework established here.

Keep the four layer stack, application, runtime, operating system, hardware, firmly in mind. It is the single most useful lens for correctly classifying any new AWS service encountered throughout the rest of this course.
This topic is now fully covered; Shared Responsibility Model, adding the security dimension to this same stack, follows immediately next.
The four layer stack introduced here will be referenced implicitly whenever a new managed service is introduced throughout the rest of this course.
Security responsibility tracks operational responsibility exactly, as the next topic makes explicit.
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: a spectrum of managed responsibility, not three isolated boxes to memorize independently.
